pedagogy.summary: A fraction a/b is understood as a copies of a unit fraction 1/b, where 1/b is the quantity made by one part when the whole is cut into b EQUAL parts. Teach the unit fraction first as an amount (a specific length/area), then build a/b by iterating (counting) that unit: 3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4. The pivotal idea is that the denominator names how many equal parts the whole is split into — and therefore the SIZE of each part — while the numerator counts how many of those parts we take. Hold the whole fixed and insist the parts be equal.
bestPractices: Introduce the unit fraction 1/b as a quantity (a definite amount/length), naming it, before non-unit fractions a/b (IES Rec 1 equal-sharing progression).
Build a/b by iterating the unit fraction — 'three-quarters is three one-quarters' — counting unit fractions the way you count objects.
Keep the whole fixed and require parts equal in AREA; accept differently-shaped pieces if they are treated as equal-area.
Vary the whole (bar, circle, length, set) and vary b so children see that the denominator controls the size of each part.
Guard against mechanical part-counting: ask 'how big is ONE part?' not only 'how many are shaded?' (IES caution that strips/circles can mislead if counted without meaning).
Link the area model, the length/number-line jump, and the set model for the same fraction so a/b is not tied to one picture.
keyRepresentations: Area model — a bar or circle partitioned into b equal parts, a shaded
Fraction strips of a single unit size
Length / number-line jump of size 1/b iterated a times
Set model — a of every b·k objects
Cuisenaire rods where a rod is chosen as the whole
commonMisconceptions: Equal-parts ignored — any b pieces are called bths regardless of size (IES Roadblock 1.2)
Counting shaded parts mechanically without grasping that numerator and denominator together name one quantity (IES caution)
Reading the denominator as a group SIZE ('thirds = groups of three') rather than the number of equal parts
Whole-number bias — a bigger denominator means a bigger part or a bigger value
Non-unit fraction taken as a unit fraction — for 3/4 shading just one part

learn.summary: Teach a/b as a copies of the unit fraction 1/b, where 1/b is the definite amount made by ONE part when a whole is cut into b EQUAL parts. Build the unit fraction first as a quantity, then iterate it (3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4). The pivotal insight is that the denominator names how many equal parts the whole is split into — and so, for a given whole, fixes the SIZE of each part — while the numerator counts how many such parts are taken. Within any comparison keep the whole fixed and insist parts be equal (equal area in area models, equal length on lengths/number lines, equal number in sets); vary b on a fixed whole so part-size visibly depends on the denominator, and vary the kind of whole across separate tasks so the idea is not tied to one picture.

activities.title: Cut it fair, then count the unit
feedback: If a learner shades without equalising the parts, ask: 'Are these parts the same size? If not, is one really one-sixth?' Have them re-cut until the parts are equal before naming any as 1/6.
If a learner says 2/6 and 2/4 are 'the same, both are 2', ask 'How big is ONE part in each bar?' and have them overlay a sixth on a fourth to see the sixth is thinner.
If a learner says 2/6 is more 'because 6 is bigger than 4', return to the overlay of one sixth on one fourth; once they see the sixth is the smaller piece, re-ask the comparison.
Reinforce correct reasoning by having them restate: 'the bottom number says how many equal parts, so it sets how big each part is.'
activities.rationale: Introducing the unit fraction as an amount and iterating it to build a/b follows the equal-sharing-before-notation progression and directly confronts whole-number bias and equal-parts errors. Requiring learners to check and re-cut until the parts are equal before labelling any as a fraction, and letting them iterate and overlay the unit themselves, is proposed to make equal-parts and unit-size felt rather than told. The side-by-side 2/6 vs 2/4 comparison with overlay targets the specific misconception that matching numerators mean equal amounts.
sourceClaims: A fraction should be understood as built from unit fractions (a/b as a copies of 1/b), taught via equal-sharing before formal notation; part-whole tools can mislead if children count parts corresponding to numerator and denominator without understanding they together name a single quantity.
Whole-number bias / larger-denominator-is-larger and equal-parts errors are documented children's fraction misconceptions.
learnerActions: Take one whole bar (a chocolate bar works well) and cut it into equal parts, e.g. 6, checking that the parts are genuinely equal in area before accepting them.
Shade ONE part and name it as a quantity: 'this is one-sixth, 1/6'.
Build 2/6, then 3/6, by copying that single 1/6 piece and counting as you go, saying 'two one-sixths, three one-sixths' and writing the label each time.
Reset the sixths bar to show 2/6, then set an identical bar beside it, cut into 4 equal parts, and shade 2 parts on it (so you have 2/6 next to 2/4).
Slide the two shaded regions over one another to compare how much chocolate each shows, and state which is more and why.
activities.intendedInsight: a/b is a copies of an equal part whose size is fixed by the denominator; shading the same NUMBER of parts does not give the same amount, because sixths are smaller than fourths of the same whole (so 2/6 < 2/4).

activities.title: How big is ONE part? (vary the whole and the denominator)
feedback: If a learner counts shaded pieces mechanically, redirect with 'how big is one part?' before accepting the answer.
If a learner thinks 1/8 > 1/4 because 8 > 4, have them cut the SAME whole into 4 then into 8 and compare one piece of each.
Accept differently-shaped pieces as equal if the learner can show they are equal in area; praise reasoning that focuses on amount rather than appearance.
activities.rationale: Linking area, length/number-line, set and Cuisenaire-rod models for one fraction prevents the concept being tied to a single representation, and varying b while holding the whole fixed makes the denominator-controls-size idea visible. Asking 'how big is one part?' guards against mechanical part-counting.
sourceClaims: A fraction should be understood as built from unit fractions (a/b as a copies of 1/b), taught via equal-sharing before formal notation; part-whole tools can mislead if children count parts corresponding to numerator and denominator without understanding they together name a single quantity.
Whole-number bias / larger-denominator-is-larger and equal-parts errors are documented children's fraction misconceptions.
learnerActions: Build the SAME fraction across different wholes — a bar, a circle, a fraction strip, a length/number line, a set of objects (e.g. 2 of every 6), and Cuisenaire rods with one chosen rod as the whole.
On a number line, make the fraction by repeating a jump of size 1/b, a times, instead of shading an area.
Re-cut one bar into 8 equal parts and name one part (1/8); compare its size to one quarter of that same bar and state which is bigger and why.
Draw a given fraction, e.g. 2/6, of the SAME whole a DIFFERENT way — differently shaped parts but the same amount.
For each model, answer not just 'how many are shaded?' but 'how big is ONE part?'
activities.intendedInsight: The same fraction names the same relationship to its whole (and the same number) whatever picture is used, but the amount it shows depends on the size of the whole; for any given whole the denominator controls how many equal parts it is cut into (regardless of that whole's shape), and more equal parts of the SAME whole means each part is smaller (1/8 < 1/4).

activities.title: Predict, then check: comparing same-numerator fractions
feedback: If the stated reason is 'the same, both are 2', after the overlay ask them to explain why 2/4 covers more despite both counting two parts.
If the reason is '6 is more so sixths-bar is more', use the overlay of one sixth on one fourth, then have them re-state the rule about part size.

For the small-bar/big-bar trap, clarify that comparing the ACTUAL amounts of chocolate requires equal wholes, while as numbers 3/4 is still greater than 1/2; praise learners who notice the wholes differ.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check routine with a reason stated before observing surfaces whole-number and part-counting reasoning diagnostically, and the physical overlay refutes both 'they're the same' and 'more parts means more'. The whole-size caveat protects against over-generalising when comparing physical amounts, without denying that fractions as numbers are comparable.

A fraction should be understood as built from unit fractions (a/b as a copies of 1/b), taught via equal-sharing before formal notation; part-whole tools can mislead if children count parts corresponding to numerator and denominator without understanding they together name a single quantity.
learnerActions: Before cutting, look at two identical bars. Predict and give a REASON: if 2 parts are shaded on a bar cut into 4, and 2 parts on an identical bar cut into 6, which shows more chocolate — or the same? State the reason out loud BEFORE observing.
Then cut both bars and slide the shaded regions over each other to check.
Revise or confirm your prediction, explaining what the comparison showed.
Build 3/4 from single pieces and say how many quarters and how big each one is.
Tackle the trap question: could 3/4 of a small bar be LESS chocolate than 1/2 of a big bar? State what must be true about the wholes to compare the amounts fairly.
activities.intendedInsight: With the whole held fixed, more equal parts means each part is smaller, so 2/4 > 2/6 and 3/4 > 3/6 even though the counts match; comparing the AMOUNTS shown by two models is only fair when the wholes are the same size, though the fractions themselves, as numbers, remain comparable (3/4 > 1/2 always).

activities.title: Identify, match and construct across models (consolidation)
feedback: For the unequal-pieces item, if a learner accepts it as quarters, overlay or measure the pieces to show they are not equal, so cannot be quarters.
A sort into equal-parts vs not can check classification, but it does not by itself show the learner can build and justify a fraction — follow matching with a construct-and-explain step.
Use evocative illustrations for recognition, but return to a measured/equal-area model whenever size is in question.
activities.rationale: Retrieval, matching and categorisation consolidate the concept once it is built, and the explicit equal-parts-vs-not sort targets the equal-parts misconception by checking classification. This supports, rather than replaces, hands-on partitioning and iterating.

Whole-number bias / larger-denominator-is-larger and equal-parts errors are documented children's fraction misconceptions.
learnerActions: Identify the fraction shaded in a given model, e.g. one shaded part of a shape in 5 equal parts named as 1/5.
Match a written fraction a/b to the model that shows it.
Sort models into 'equal parts' vs 'not equal parts', and judge whether a bar cut into 4 UNEQUAL pieces with one shaded really shows a quarter.
Construct a requested fraction yourself — draw it, or choose/colour the right number of equal parts.
Explain in words what the denominator and numerator each tell you for one chosen example.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure, flexible recognition and construction of a/b across representations, with equal parts as the non-negotiable criterion.

constraints: Always hold the whole fixed and require parts to be equal when naming fractions: equal in AREA for area models, equal in length for length/number-line models, equal in number for set models; differently-shaped pieces of an area model are acceptable only if they are genuinely equal in area.
Introduce the unit fraction 1/b as a named quantity before non-unit fractions a/b.

When comparing the AMOUNTS two models show by counting shaded parts, this is only valid when the wholes are the same size; state this explicitly, especially in trap questions mixing a small and a large whole. Note that fractions as numbers remain comparable regardless (3/4 > 1/2).

A static reference such as a fraction wall can label parts ('one of six equal parts = 1/6') but does not let the learner enforce equal parts or iterate the unit themselves; treat it as a reference layer alongside active partitioning, not a substitute for it.

Recognition-only tasks (identify/match) and sorts confirm classification/fluency but do not by themselves elicit independent construction or justification; pair them with a construct-and-explain step.

Keep the work in the plane (area/length/set); a third spatial dimension is not needed for this planar concept and can obscure equal-area partitioning. This is a scoped limitation here, not a universal claim about 3D media.
Guard against mechanical part-counting: routinely ask 'how big is ONE part?', not only 'how many are shaded?'
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source assessment's worked comparison is sound: with the whole fixed, 3/6 < 3/4 and 2/6 < 2/4 because more equal parts makes each part smaller. These were preserved as the target reasoning.

The whole-size 'fair comparison' caveat applies to comparing physical amounts across different-sized wholes; the fractions themselves as numbers remain comparable (3/4 > 1/2). This scoping was added to avoid implying fractions are not comparable, and Activity 2's part-size claim was tightened to a FIXED whole to match it.
Cuisenaire rods and fraction strips from the source key representations were restored in Activity 2, which an earlier draft had dropped.
The England National Curriculum Year 3 placement claim is marked verified:false in the source; treat the age mapping (ages 8–9 / Year 3) as unconfirmed.

Source claims about equal-sharing progression and documented misconceptions support the general teaching principles cited; they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific activity or interactive format proposed here.

The original research rated non-interactive and 3D/dialogue formats as poor fit with strong wording (e.g. 'adds nothing', 'where the learning happens'); these were softened to scoped affordance/limit statements in constraints rather than treated as universal pedagogical laws.

assess.poeTask: Before cutting, show two identical bars. Ask the child to PREDICT and give a REASON: if I shade 2 parts of a bar cut into 4, and 2 parts of an identical bar cut into 6, which shows more chocolate — or the same? The reason stated before observing is the diagnostic part. Then cut and slide the two shaded regions over each other: 2/4 covers more than 2/6, refuting both 'the same, both are 2' and '6 is more'.
probeDeeper: Build 3/4 for me from single pieces — how many quarters, and how big is each one?
If I cut the same bar into 8 equal parts instead of 4, what is one part called, and is it bigger or smaller than one quarter?
Could 3/4 of this small bar be less chocolate than 1/2 of that big bar? What has to be true about the wholes for us to compare fairly?
Draw 2/6 a different way — a different shape, but the same amount.
assess.correctAnswer: 3/4. The 4 (denominator) tells how many EQUAL parts the whole is cut into, so each part is 1/4; the 3 (numerator) counts how many of those parts we take, i.e. 3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4. The second bar shows 3/6, which is LESS than 3/4: both have 3 shaded parts, but each sixth is smaller than each fourth because the same whole is cut into more pieces.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — 'the second one is more because it has sixths and 6 is bigger than 4'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to identical wholes; overlay one sixth on one fourth so the child sees the sixth is the smaller piece; only then re-ask the comparison
errorPatterns.distractor: 3/6 is more — it's in sixths and 6 is more than 4
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 3/6 > 3/4, pointing to the larger denominator as the larger amount

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts shaded parts and ignores their size — 'they're the same, both have 3 pieces shaded'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'how big is ONE part in each bar?'; overlay a sixth on a fourth; establish that same count of different-sized parts is not the same amount
errorPatterns.distractor: They're the same — both have 3 pieces shaded
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says equal because the numerators match, without attending to part size

errorPatterns.pattern: Equal-parts ignored — describes the denominator as 'cut into 4 pieces' with no requirement they be equal
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a bar cut into 4 UNEQUAL pieces with one shaded and ask if that shaded piece is a quarter; establish equal-area as the criterion
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When explaining what the 4 means, omits 'equal'; would accept a 4-unequal-piece bar as showing quarters

responseLevels.gap: Reads numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers; counts shaded pieces; says 3/6 equals or beats 3/4; cannot say how big one part is.
responseLevels.full: Names 3/4 as three copies of 1/4, explains the denominator sets the equal-part SIZE while the numerator counts them, and concludes 3/6 < 3/4 because sixths are smaller than fourths of the same whole; transfers by redrawing 2/6 a different way.
responseLevels.partial: Names 3/4 correctly and says '4 parts, 3 shaded', but handles the comparison by counting or whole-number reasoning, or can name the parts without explaining that each 1/b's size depends on b — listing the parts without relating part-size to the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a bar cut into 4 equal parts with 3 shaded. Ask: 'What fraction is shaded? In your own words, what does the 4 tell us and what does the 3 tell us?' Then show an identical bar cut into 6 equal parts with 3 shaded and ask: 'Is this more chocolate, less, or the same as the first — and why?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands a/b as a copies of a unit whose size is set by b will say 3/6 < 3/4 and justify by part size; a child using whole-number or part-counting reasoning will call them equal ('both have 3') or say 3/6 is more ('6 is bigger'). It is hard to answer 'less, because sixths are smaller' for the wrong reason, and hard to answer 'equal/more' if you truly grasp unit-part size.
